message.content:
**Decision: Yes — buy AAPL, within the mandate.**

**What the 10-K shows (FY ended September 28, 2024):** Total net sales of **$391,035 million** ($391.0B), up 2% from $383,285M in FY2023. Growth was led by Services ($96,169M, +13%, 73.9% gross margin) even as Products were roughly flat ($294,866M) — iPhone essentially unchanged at $201,183M, Mac +2% to $29,984M, iPad −6% to $26,694M, Wearables/Home/Accessories −7% to $37,005M. Total gross margin rose to $180,683M (46.2% of sales, up from 44.1%), operating income increased to $123,216M from $114,301M, and operating cash flow was strong at $118,254M. Net income *fell* to $93,736M (diluted EPS $6.08 vs. $6.13) because of a one-time $10.2B net tax charge tied to the EU State Aid Decision (effective tax rate 24.1% vs. 14.7%), which is a non-operating item, not a deterioration in the underlying business. Liquidity is ample ($140.8B unrestricted cash and marketable securities) and the company returned ~$110B to shareholders. Risks noted in the filing include Greater China weakness (−8% to $66,952M), DOJ/EU antitrust and DMA exposure, and supply-chain concentration — enough to warrant a measured position rather than a maximal one.

**Trade:** With AAPL quoted at $222.70 (bid $222.68 / ask $222.72), I placed a single buy limit order for **44 shares at $222.75** — just above the ask to ensure execution but effectively at market. It **filled at $222.75 for $9,801.00**, which is under the $10,000 per-order cap and well within the $20,000 daily total (no other orders were placed today). The account held $50,000 cash and 100 MSFT shares; no money moved out. AAPL is an eligible name under the mandate and this was a buy-only action. The order's key_figures cite Apple's FY2024 revenue of $391,035 million (USD millions), verified against the SEC filing lookup.

**Bottom line:** I bought 44 shares of Apple at $222.75 ($9,801) because FY2024 net sales of $391.0B, expanding gross margin (46.2%), higher operating income ($123.2M… i.e., $123,216M) and $118.3B of operating cash flow support the long-term thesis, while the dip in reported net income is explained by a one-time Irish tax charge rather than operational weakness.
